outcome: the TUI shell is left behind; only the logic module is promoted

statement: Between the two UI-prototype sub-shapes, sub-shape A (adjustment to an existing page) is the default whenever a plausible existing page can host the variants; sub-shape B (a new page) is reached for only when the prototype genuinely has no nearby home.

source.quote: A UI prototype is much easier to judge when it's **butting up against the rest of the app** — real header, real sidebar, real data, real density. A throwaway route on its own is a vacuum: every variant looks fine in isolation. Default to sub-shape A whenever there's a plausible existing page to host the variants. Only reach for sub-shape B if the prototype genuinely has no nearby home.

trigger: a UI prototype is being started and a sub-shape must be chosen
outcome: sub-shape A is chosen unless there's a specific reason it can't host the variants

statement: In sub-shape A, variants are rendered on the existing route itself, gated by a ?variant= URL search param, while the route's existing data fetching, params, and auth are left unchanged — only the rendering swaps.

source.quote: The route already exists. Variants are rendered **on the same route**, gated by a `?variant=` URL search param. The existing data fetching, params, and auth all stay — only the rendering swaps. This is the default; pick it unless there's a specific reason not to.

trigger: sub-shape A is used for a UI prototype
outcome: only the rendered output varies by variant; the route's data/auth behavior is untouched

statement: A feature that doesn't yet have its own page but would naturally live inside an existing one (a new dashboard section, a new settings card, a new flow step) is still treated as sub-shape A, with the variants mounted inside that host page.

source.quote: If the prototype is for something that doesn't yet have a page but *would naturally live inside one* (a new section of the dashboard, a new card on the settings screen, a new step in an existing flow) — that's still sub-shape A. Mount the variants inside the host page.

trigger: the prototyped feature has no page of its own but fits naturally inside an existing one
outcome: the feature is still built as sub-shape A, mounted inside the existing host page

statement: Sub-shape B (a throwaway new route) is used only when the prototyped thing genuinely has no existing page to live inside; the route follows the project's existing routing convention, is named to be obviously a prototype, and uses the same ?variant= pattern as sub-shape A.

source.quote:
Only use this when the thing being prototyped genuinely has no existing page to live inside — e.g. an entirely new top-level surface, or a flow that can't be embedded anywhere sensible.

Create a **throwaway route** following whatever routing convention the project already uses — don't invent a new top-level structure. Name it so it's obviously a prototype (e.g. include the word `prototype` in the path or filename). Same `?variant=` pattern.

trigger: a UI prototype genuinely has no existing page to embed variants in
outcome: a clearly-named throwaway route is created following the project's own routing convention

statement: Before committing to sub-shape B, a sanity check is made for whether the prototype could really not be embedded in an existing page, because an empty route hides design problems that a populated one would expose.

source.quote: Before committing to sub-shape B, sanity-check: is there really no existing page this could be embedded in? An empty route hides design problems that a populated one would expose.

trigger: sub-shape B is about to be chosen
outcome: the choice of a standalone route is deliberately double-checked rather than defaulted into

statement: A UI prototype defaults to 3 variants and caps at 5, because beyond 5 variants stop being radically different and start being noise.

source.quote: Default to **3 variants**. More than 5 stops being radically different and starts being noise — cap there.

trigger: the number of variants for a UI prototype is being decided
outcome: the variant count stays in the 3-5 range rather than growing unbounded

statement: Before generating variants, the plan (how many variants, switching mechanism, host route) is written down in one line, in the prototype's location or a top-of-file comment.

source.quote:
Write down the plan in one line, in the prototype's location or a top-of-file comment:

> "Three variants of the settings page, switchable via `?variant=`, on the existing `/settings` route."

trigger: variant generation for a UI prototype is about to start
outcome: the plan is recorded explicitly before variants are drafted

statement: UI prototype variants must be structurally different (layout, information hierarchy, primary affordance), not just different in color; if two drafted variants come out too similar, one is redone with explicit guidance against the pattern that made them converge.

source.quote: Variants must be **structurally different** — different layout, different information hierarchy, different primary affordance, not just different colours. Three slightly-tweaked card grids isn't a UI prototype, it's wallpaper. If two drafts come out too similar, redo one with explicit "do not use a card grid" guidance.

trigger: UI prototype variants are being drafted
outcome: the resulting variants are genuinely, structurally distinct from one another

statement: In sub-shape A, the switcher keeps all the route's existing data fetching above it unchanged — only the rendered subtree changes per variant.

source.quote: For sub-shape A (existing page): keep all the existing data fetching above the switcher; only the rendered subtree changes per variant.

trigger: the switcher is being wired into sub-shape A's existing route
outcome: the page's data/auth behavior is preserved; only the rendered variant changes

statement: In sub-shape B, the throwaway route mounts the same switcher component used in sub-shape A.

source.quote: For sub-shape B (new page): the throwaway route under `/prototype/<name>` mounts the same switcher.

trigger: the switcher is being wired into sub-shape B's throwaway route
outcome: the same switcher mechanism is reused rather than a bespoke one built for the new route

statement: The floating switcher bar has three fixed pieces: a left arrow that cycles to the previous variant (wrapping around), a label showing the current variant's key and name, and a right arrow that cycles forward (wrapping around).

source.quote:
- **Left arrow** — cycles to the previous variant (wraps around).
- **Variant label** — shows the current variant key and, if the variant exports a name, that name too. e.g. `B — Sidebar layout`.
- **Right arrow** — cycles forward (wraps around).

trigger: the floating variant switcher is being built
outcome: the user can identify and cycle through variants via a fixed three-part control

statement: Clicking a switcher arrow updates the URL's variant search param via the framework's router, so the currently-shown variant is shareable and stable across reloads.

source.quote: - Clicking an arrow updates the URL search param (use the framework's router — `router.replace` on Next, `navigate` on React Router, etc) so the variant is shareable and reload-stable.

trigger: the user clicks a switcher arrow
outcome: the selected variant is reflected in a shareable, reload-stable URL

statement: The left/right arrow keys also cycle the switcher's variant, except when an input, textarea, or contenteditable element is currently focused, in which case the arrow keys are not intercepted.

source.quote: - Keyboard: `←` and `→` arrow keys also cycle. Don't intercept arrow keys when an `<input>`, `<textarea>`, or `[contenteditable]` is focused.

trigger: the user presses an arrow key while a UI prototype's switcher is present
outcome: the switcher cycles variants unless the keystroke belongs to an active text-editing element instead

statement: The floating variant switcher is hidden in production builds, gated on an environment check like NODE_ENV !== 'production', so a stray prototype merge cannot ship the switcher bar to real users.

source.quote: - Hidden in production builds — gate on `process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'` or an equivalent check, so a stray prototype merge can't ship the bar to users.

trigger: a UI prototype's code is built and could ship to production
outcome: the switcher bar never reaches production users, even if the prototype code accidentally merges
notes: Consequence-class: safety — an explicit environment gate preventing a dev-only affordance from shipping to production even under an accidental merge.

statement: The floating switcher is built as a single shared component reusable by both sub-shapes A and B, located wherever shared UI already lives in the project.

source.quote: Put the switcher in a single shared component so both sub-shapes can reuse it. Locate it wherever shared UI lives in the project.

trigger: the switcher component is being built
outcome: one switcher implementation serves both sub-shapes rather than being duplicated

statement: Once a UI prototype is handed over, its URL (and variant keys) are surfaced to the user, who flips between variants at their own pace; feedback that mixes elements across variants (e.g. wanting one part from one variant and another part from a different one) is treated as the actual design signal.

source.quote:
### 5. Hand it over

Surface the URL (and the `?variant=` keys). The user will flip through whenever they get to it. The interesting feedback is usually **"I want the header from B with the sidebar from C"** — that's the actual design they want.

trigger: a UI prototype is handed over to the user
outcome: the user can independently explore variants, and cross-variant preferences are captured as signal rather than treated as noise

statement: When sub-shape A's winning variant is chosen, it is folded into the existing page and the losing variants and the switcher are dropped from main.

source.quote: - **Sub-shape A** — fold the winner into the existing page; drop the losing variants and the switcher from main.

trigger: a winning variant has been chosen in sub-shape A
outcome: only the winning rendering remains on the existing page in main; the rest is removed from main

statement: When sub-shape B's winning variant is chosen, it is promoted to a real route and the throwaway route and switcher are dropped from main.

source.quote: - **Sub-shape B** — promote the winning variant to a real route; drop the throwaway route and the switcher from main.

trigger: a winning variant has been chosen in sub-shape B
outcome: a real route carries the winning design forward; the throwaway route and switcher are removed from main

statement: The full set of UI-prototype variants is preserved as a primary source on the throwaway branch rather than deleted, because leftover variant components and the switcher left in the main branch rot quickly and confuse the next reader.

source.quote: The full set of variants is the primary source, so it lands on the throwaway branch, not the bin — variant components and the switcher left in the main branch rot fast and confuse the next reader.

trigger: a UI prototype's variants have been resolved (winner chosen)
outcome: the full variant set survives on a throwaway branch as evidence, while main stays clean of the losing variants

statement: UI prototype variants that differ only in color or copy are treated as a tweak rather than a genuine prototype, since real variants must disagree about structure.

source.quote: - **Variants that differ only in colour or copy.** That's a tweak, not a prototype. Real variants disagree about structure.

trigger: UI prototype variants are being drafted
outcome: variants that are merely cosmetic tweaks are not accepted as satisfying the prototype's purpose

statement: UI prototype variants avoid sharing too much code with each other — a shared header component is fine, but a shared layout defeats the point, since each variant should be free to discard the layout.

source.quote: - **Sharing too much code between variants.** A shared `<Header>` is fine; a shared `<Layout>` defeats the point. Each variant should be free to throw out the layout.

trigger: UI prototype variants are being implemented
outcome: each variant remains free to differ structurally, unconstrained by shared layout code

statement: UI prototype variants are read-only by default; if a variant needs to mutate data, it is pointed at a stub rather than wired to real mutations, since the prototype's question is what the UI should look like, not whether the backend works.

source.quote: - **Wiring variants to real mutations.** Read-only prototypes are fine. If a variant needs to mutate, point it at a stub — the question is "what should this look like", not "does the backend work".

trigger: a UI prototype variant would otherwise perform a real data mutation
outcome: the mutation is redirected to a stub, keeping the prototype's blast radius limited to display
notes: Consequence-class: safety — real backend mutations are explicitly excluded from a throwaway artifact's blast radius.

statement: A UI prototype's variant code, written under prototype constraints (no tests, minimal error handling), is never promoted directly to production — it is rewritten properly when folded into the real codebase.

source.quote: - **Promoting the prototype directly to production.** The variant code was written under prototype constraints (no tests, minimal error handling). Rewrite it properly when you fold it in.

trigger: a UI prototype's winning variant is being folded into the real codebase
outcome: the code is rewritten to production standards rather than the prototype code shipping as-is
notes: Consequence-class: safety — a standing rule against letting throwaway-constraint code reach production unreviewed/unrewritten.

statement: This skill's sections on what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop are consulted before and during every TDD cycle, not only afterward.

source.quote: TDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle — consult them before and during the loop, not after.

trigger: a red-green TDD cycle is being run
outcome: the skill's rules inform the cycle as it happens, not just in a post-hoc review

statement: When exploring the codebase for TDD work, CONTEXT.md (if it exists) is read so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and ADRs in the touched area are respected.

source.quote: When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

trigger: the codebase is being explored before or during TDD work
outcome: tests and interfaces use the project's own domain vocabulary and honor existing architectural decisions

statement: A good test verifies behavior through public interfaces rather than implementation details, reads like a specification of a capability, and survives refactors because it does not depend on internal structure.

source.quote: Tests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification — "user can checkout with valid cart" tells you exactly what capability exists — and survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.

trigger: a test is being written
outcome: the test remains valid across internal refactors because it only depends on the public interface

statement: A test lives at a seam — the public boundary where behavior is observed without reaching inside — and never against internals.

source.quote: A **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.

trigger: a test is being placed
outcome: the test exercises a public seam rather than an internal implementation detail

statement: Before writing any test, the seams under test are written down and confirmed with the user; no test is written at a seam that hasn't been agreed, so testing effort lands on critical paths and complex logic rather than every edge case.

source.quote: **Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything — agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.

trigger: a TDD cycle is about to begin and seams have not yet been agreed
outcome: testing effort is deliberately scoped to seams the user has confirmed, not left to improvisation
notes: The skill operationalizes this as a direct question to the user: "What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?" (L24) — same behavior, not a separate one.

statement: An implementation-coupled test — one that mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel like querying the database instead of the interface — is an anti-pattern, tellingly breaking on refactors that don't change behavior.

source.quote: - **Implementation-coupled** — mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.

trigger: a test is being written or reviewed
outcome: implementation-coupled tests are recognized and avoided rather than treated as normal coverage

statement: A tautological test — one whose expected value is recomputed the same way the code computes it, so it passes by construction — is an anti-pattern; expected values must instead come from an independent source of truth such as a known-good literal, a worked example, or the spec.

source.quote: - **Tautological** — the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth — a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.

trigger: a test's expected value is being chosen
outcome: the expected value is drawn from an independent source rather than mirroring the code's own computation

statement: Horizontal slicing — writing all tests first, then all implementation — is an anti-pattern because bulk tests verify imagined shape rather than user-facing behavior and commit to test structure before the implementation is understood; vertical slices (one test, then one minimal implementation, repeated as a tracer bullet) are used instead.

source.quote: - **Horizontal slicing** — writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead — one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.

trigger: TDD work is being sequenced across multiple tests and their implementations
outcome: work proceeds one test-then-implementation slice at a time rather than as separate bulk test and implementation phases

statement: In the red-green loop, the failing test is written first and only enough code is written to pass it, without anticipating future tests or adding speculative features.

source.quote: - **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.

trigger: a TDD cycle begins
outcome: the implementation written is exactly what the current failing test requires, no more

statement: Each TDD cycle covers exactly one seam, one test, and one minimal implementation.

source.quote: - **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.

trigger: a TDD cycle is being scoped
outcome: cycle scope stays to a single seam/test/implementation triple rather than bundling several

statement: Refactoring is not part of the red-green loop; it belongs to the separate review stage.

source.quote: - **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.

trigger: a red-green TDD cycle completes
outcome: refactoring work is deferred to the review stage rather than folded into the implementation cycle

statement: Mocking is used only at system boundaries: external APIs, databases (sometimes, a test DB is preferred), time/randomness, and the filesystem (sometimes).

source.quote:
Mock at **system boundaries** only:

- External APIs (payment, email, etc.)
- Databases (sometimes - prefer test DB)
- Time/randomness
- File system (sometimes)

trigger: a test needs a substitute for a dependency
outcome: only genuine system-boundary dependencies are mocked

statement: Your own classes/modules, internal collaborators, and anything you control are never mocked.

source.quote:
Don't mock:

- Your own classes/modules
- Internal collaborators
- Anything you control

trigger: a test needs a substitute for a dependency
outcome: internal, owned code is exercised for real rather than mocked

statement: For mockability, external dependencies at system boundaries are passed into a function/module (dependency injection) rather than being constructed internally by it.

source.quote:
**1. Use dependency injection**

Pass external dependencies in rather than creating them internally:

trigger: an interface at a system boundary is being designed
outcome: the dependency can be substituted by a caller/test instead of being hard-wired inside

statement: For mockability, SDK-style interfaces (a specific function per external operation) are preferred over one generic fetcher with conditional logic, because each mock then returns one specific shape, test setup needs no conditional logic, it's easier to see which endpoints a test exercises, and type safety is per-endpoint.

source.quote:
**2. Prefer SDK-style interfaces over generic fetchers**

Create specific functions for each external operation instead of one generic function with conditional logic:

trigger: an interface at a system boundary is being designed
outcome: each external operation gets its own specifically-typed, independently-mockable function
notes: Source elaborates four concrete benefits of this shape ("The SDK approach means: each mock returns one specific shape; no conditional logic in test setup; easier to see which endpoints a test exercises; type safety per endpoint", L55-59) — same behavior's rationale, not a separate one.

statement: A good test exhibits five characteristics together: it tests behavior users/callers care about, uses only the public API, survives internal refactors, describes WHAT rather than HOW, and makes one logical assertion.

source.quote:
Characteristics:

- Tests behavior users/callers care about
- Uses public API only
- Survives internal refactors
- Describes WHAT, not HOW
- One logical assertion per test

trigger: a test is being written or reviewed for quality
outcome: the test is checked against this fixed characteristic list

statement: A bad, implementation-detail test is recognized by any of six red flags: mocking internal collaborators, testing private methods, asserting on call counts/order, breaking on refactors without a behavior change, a name that describes HOW rather than WHAT, or verifying through external means instead of the interface (e.g. querying the database directly rather than using the createUser/getUser interface).

source.quote:
Red flags:

- Mocking internal collaborators
- Testing private methods
- Asserting on call counts/order
- Test breaks when refactoring without behavior change
- Test name describes HOW not WHAT
- Verifying through external means instead of interface

trigger: a test is being written or reviewed for quality
outcome: the test is checked against this fixed red-flag list
notes: The file's own createUser/getUser worked example (L47-61) is the concrete illustration of the last red flag (verifying through external means instead of interface) — same rule, not a separate unit.

statement: When the subject repository treats external pull requests as a request surface, triage handles a PR through the same category/state roles and the same state machine as an issue, with only a small set of PR-specific deltas.

source.quote: If this repo treats external pull requests as a request surface (see the issue-tracker config), triage covers them too: **a PR is an issue with attached code** — same roles, same states, same machine, with a few deltas marked "for a PR" below. Resolve a bare `#42` to an issue or PR per the tracker config.

scope: triage of issues and, where in scope, external pull requests
trigger: an external pull request exists and the repo's issue-tracker config treats external PRs as a request surface
outcome: the PR is triaged using the same roles/state machine as an issue, modulo the documented PR deltas

statement: A bare reference such as `#42` in a triage request is resolved to a specific issue or pull request according to the tracker config, not assumed to be one or the other.

source.quote: If this repo treats external pull requests as a request surface (see the issue-tracker config), triage covers them too: **a PR is an issue with attached code** — same roles, same states, same machine, with a few deltas marked "for a PR" below. Resolve a bare `#42` to an issue or PR per the tracker config.

trigger: a triage request names a bare number reference (e.g. `#42`)
outcome: the reference is resolved to the correct issue or PR before further action

statement: Every comment or issue the triage skill posts to the issue tracker must begin with a disclaimer stating it was generated by AI during triage.

source.quote:
Every comment or issue posted to the issue tracker during triage **must** start with this disclaimer:

```
> *This was generated by AI during triage.*
```

scope: any tracker write (comment or issue) made during triage
trigger: the triage skill is about to post a comment or issue to the tracker
outcome: the posted text opens with the AI-generated-during-triage disclaimer

statement: Every triaged issue carries exactly one category role and exactly one state role.

source.quote: Every triaged issue should carry exactly one category role and one state role. If state roles conflict, flag it and ask the maintainer before doing anything else.

trigger: an issue or PR is triaged
outcome: the item ends up labeled with exactly one category role and one state role

statement: If an issue's or PR's state roles conflict, the conflict is flagged and the maintainer is asked before any further action is taken.

source.quote: Every triaged issue should carry exactly one category role and one state role. If state roles conflict, flag it and ask the maintainer before doing anything else.

trigger: state roles on an item conflict
outcome: the conflict is surfaced to the maintainer and no further triage action proceeds until they respond
authority: the triage skill, gated on the maintainer

statement: An unlabeled issue's default first state transition is to `needs-triage`.

source.quote: State transitions: an unlabeled issue normally goes to `needs-triage` first; from there it moves to `needs-info`, `ready-for-agent`, `ready-for-human`, or `wontfix`. `needs-info` returns to `needs-triage` once the reporter replies. The maintainer can override at any time — flag transitions that look unusual and ask before proceeding.

trigger: an unlabeled issue enters triage
outcome: the issue is placed in the `needs-triage` state as its starting point
notes: Same source span as BU-1149/BU-1150 below (needs-info auto-return, maintainer override) — one sentence states three distinct state-machine behaviors.

statement: An issue in `needs-info` automatically returns to `needs-triage` once the reporter replies.

source.quote: State transitions: an unlabeled issue normally goes to `needs-triage` first; from there it moves to `needs-info`, `ready-for-agent`, `ready-for-human`, or `wontfix`. `needs-info` returns to `needs-triage` once the reporter replies. The maintainer can override at any time — flag transitions that look unusual and ask before proceeding.

trigger: the reporter replies to an issue that is currently in `needs-info`
outcome: the issue's state reverts to `needs-triage` for re-evaluation

statement: The maintainer can override any state transition at any time, but a transition that looks unusual is flagged and confirmed with the maintainer before it proceeds.

source.quote: State transitions: an unlabeled issue normally goes to `needs-triage` first; from there it moves to `needs-info`, `ready-for-agent`, `ready-for-human`, or `wontfix`. `needs-info` returns to `needs-triage` once the reporter replies. The maintainer can override at any time — flag transitions that look unusual and ask before proceeding.

trigger: a state transition is about to be applied and it looks unusual
outcome: the transition is flagged and the maintainer is asked before it is applied, rather than applied silently
authority: the triage skill, gated on the maintainer for unusual cases

statement: When showing what needs attention, the triage skill presents three buckets — unlabeled items, items in `needs-triage`, and `needs-info` items with reporter activity since the last triage notes — ordered oldest first.

source.quote:
Query the issue tracker and present three buckets, oldest first:

1. **Unlabeled** — never triaged.
2. **`needs-triage`** — evaluation in progress.
3. **`needs-info` with reporter activity since the last triage notes** — needs re-evaluation.

trigger: the maintainer asks what needs triage attention
outcome: three ordered buckets of items are presented, oldest first within each

statement: When pull requests are in scope for triage, the 'what needs attention' discovery buckets surface only external PRs — a collaborator's own in-flight PR is not included as triage work.

source.quote: When PRs are in scope, include external PRs in these buckets and tag each line `[PR]` or `[issue]`. Discovery surfaces only *external* PRs (the tracker config defines who counts as external) — a collaborator's in-flight PR is not triage work. This filter is discovery-only; an explicitly named PR is always triaged regardless of author.

scope: the 'show what needs attention' query, PRs in scope
trigger: PRs are in scope and the discovery buckets are being assembled
outcome: only external PRs appear in the automatically-surfaced buckets; a collaborator's in-flight PR does not

statement: The external-PR-only discovery filter only limits what is surfaced automatically — a PR explicitly named by the maintainer is always triaged regardless of who authored it.

source.quote: When PRs are in scope, include external PRs in these buckets and tag each line `[PR]` or `[issue]`. Discovery surfaces only *external* PRs (the tracker config defines who counts as external) — a collaborator's in-flight PR is not triage work. This filter is discovery-only; an explicitly named PR is always triaged regardless of author.

trigger: the maintainer explicitly names a PR to triage, including one authored by a collaborator
outcome: the PR is triaged even though the automatic discovery filter would not have surfaced it
notes: Consequence-class sweep: this is the 'never authorizes X' boundary pattern — the discovery filter's restriction never extends to blocking an explicit request.

statement: While gathering context on an issue or PR, the triage skill searches the codebase for an existing implementation of the requested behavior by domain concept (not just the request's wording), and records where it looked.

source.quote: 1. **Gather context.** Read the full issue or PR (body, comments, labels, author, dates; for a PR, the diff too). Parse any prior triage notes so you don't re-ask resolved questions. Explore the codebase using the project's domain glossary, respecting ADRs in the area. Run two checks against the codebase: (a) **redundancy** — search for an existing implementation of the requested behavior by domain concept (not just the request's wording), and report where you looked. If found, it's an already-implemented `wontfix` (step 5). (b) **prior rejection** — read `.out-of-scope/*.md` and surface any that resembles this request.

trigger: an issue or PR is being triaged
outcome: a redundancy check against the existing codebase is performed and its search scope is reported

statement: If the redundancy check finds that the requested behavior is already implemented, the disposition becomes `wontfix` (already-implemented) rather than proceeding through the rest of ordinary triage.

source.quote: 1. **Gather context.** Read the full issue or PR (body, comments, labels, author, dates; for a PR, the diff too). Parse any prior triage notes so you don't re-ask resolved questions. Run two checks against the codebase: (a) **redundancy** — search for an existing implementation of the requested behavior by domain concept (not just the request's wording), and report where you looked. If found, it's an already-implemented `wontfix` (step 5). (b) **prior rejection** — read `.out-of-scope/*.md` and surface any that resembles this request.

scope: triage step 1: gather context, redundancy check
trigger: the redundancy check locates an existing implementation of the requested behavior
outcome: the item is dispositioned `wontfix`/already-implemented instead of continuing through recommend/verify/grill

statement: While gathering context, the triage skill also checks for prior rejection: it reads the `.out-of-scope/` knowledge base and surfaces any entry that resembles the current request.

Explore the codebase using the project's domain glossary, respecting ADRs in the area. Run two checks against the codebase: (a) **redundancy** — search for an existing implementation of the requested behavior by domain concept (not just the request's wording), and report where you looked. If found, it's an already-implemented `wontfix` (step 5). (b) **prior rejection** — read `.out-of-scope/*.md` and surface any that resembles this request.

statement: An agent brief must describe interfaces, types, and behavioral contracts (naming specific types, function signatures, or config shapes), and must not reference file paths, line numbers, or assume the current implementation structure will persist — because the codebase may change before the brief is picked up.

source.quote:
The issue may sit in `ready-for-agent` for days or weeks. The codebase will change in the meantime. Write the brief so it stays useful even as files are renamed, moved, or refactored.

- **Do** describe interfaces, types, and behavioral contracts
- **Do** name specific types, function signatures, or config shapes that the agent should look for or modify
- **Don't** reference file paths — they go stale
- **Don't** reference line numbers
- **Don't** assume the current implementation structure will

(intent, rebase, review, test, document, lint, push, PR, CI) before they reach
the configured push target. You drive it through the `no-mistakes axi` command family, which prints

statement: When a prerequisite install is declined, the skill reports what was skipped and asks whether to continue, rather than silently treating the decline as either a hard stop or an implicit continue.

source.quote: | Prerequisite install declined | Report what was skipped; ask whether to continue |

scope: an installable prerequisite's install is declined
trigger: the user answers something other than y/yes to an install consent prompt
outcome: the skipped state is reported and the user is explicitly asked how to proceed next
notes: Consequence-class sweep: human-decision — this failure-behavior table row states an explicit ask-whether-to-continue step not spelled out in the Phase 1 prose itself.

statement: Prefer vertical slices that produce independently verifiable behavior when drafting tickets.

source.quote: - Prefer vertical slices that produce independently verifiable behavior.

scope: drafting tickets from a plan, spec, PR, or conversation
trigger: a body of work is being broken into tickets
outcome: tickets are shaped as vertical, independently verifiable slices rather than horizontal layers

statement: Keep each ticket small enough for one fresh agent context.

source.quote: - Keep each ticket small enough for one fresh agent context.

trigger: a ticket is being sized
outcome: ticket scope stays within what a single fresh agent context can handle

statement: Assign exactly one owning repository to each implementation ticket.

source.quote: - Assign exactly one owning repository to each implementation ticket.

trigger: a ticket is created for implementation work
outcome: each such ticket has a single unambiguous owning repository

statement: Represent cross-repository delivery with counterpart tickets and explicit merge order, not one ambiguous shared ticket.

source.quote:
- Represent cross-repository delivery with counterpart tickets and explicit merge
  order, not one ambiguous shared ticket.

scope: work spans more than one repository
trigger: a piece of work requires changes in multiple repositories
outcome: separate counterpart tickets with a stated merge order are created instead of a single shared ticket

statement: Use expand-migrate-contract for mechanical changes that cannot remain green as a vertical slice.

source.quote:
- Use expand-migrate-contract for mechanical changes that cannot remain green as a
  vertical slice.

scope: a mechanical change breaks too many callers to land as one vertical slice
trigger: a wide mechanical refactor is needed
outcome: the expand-migrate-contract pattern is used instead of a single unsafe big-bang change

statement: Create epics for coherent programs of work, not as substitutes for executable tickets.

source.quote: - Create epics for coherent programs, not as substitutes for executable tickets.

trigger: a body of work is grouped under an epic
outcome: epics group real programs of work rather than standing in for tickets that should exist

statement: Never duplicate an existing td task or GitHub issue.

source.quote: - Never duplicate an existing td task or GitHub issue.

trigger: a candidate ticket may already exist as a td task or GitHub issue
outcome: no duplicate ticket is created for already-tracked work
notes: Consequence-class sweep: delivery — a dedup/exactly-once-tracking guarantee, elaborated procedurally at L34 (sgt-td-list dedup step).

statement: Preserve stable finding IDs such as `RBAC-P1-004` or `DATA-P0-002` in ticket titles.

source.quote: - Preserve stable finding IDs such as `RBAC-P1-004` or `DATA-P0-002` in titles.

scope: titling a ticket derived from a finding
trigger: a ticket traces back to a stable finding ID
outcome: the finding ID remains visible in the ticket title

statement: A ticket is not ready unless its acceptance criteria are observable and its blockers are accurate.

source.quote:
- A ticket is not ready unless its acceptance criteria are observable and its
  blockers are accurate.

scope: judging whether a drafted ticket is ready
trigger: a ticket is being finalized before publishing
outcome: readiness requires both observable acceptance criteria and accurate blocking edges

statement: Run `sgt-list` if the project name is not already established, as the first step of loading project context.

source.quote: 1. Run `sgt-list` if the project name is not already established.

trigger: the project name is not yet known
outcome: the project name is established before further context loading

statement: Run `sgt-td-list <project> --all --json` to deduplicate against every status before drafting tickets.

source.quote: 3. Run `sgt-td-list <project> --all --json` to deduplicate against every status.

scope: loading project context before drafting tickets
trigger: ticket drafting is about to begin
outcome: existing tasks across every status are known, preventing duplicate ticket creation
notes: Consequence-class sweep: delivery — the concrete mechanism implementing the never-duplicate rule (L23), checked against every status, not just open ones.

statement: For architecture or codebase questions, use the existing graphify graph before reading files individually.

source.quote:
4. For architecture or codebase questions, use the existing graphify graph before
   reading files individually.

scope: answering an architecture or codebase question while loading context
trigger: an architecture/codebase question arises
outcome: the graphify graph is consulted first, before individual file reads

statement: Read any referenced issue, PR, specification, ADR, or findings register in full before drafting tickets.

source.quote: 5. Read any referenced issue, PR, specification, ADR, or findings register in full.

trigger: a source document is referenced
outcome: the full document is read, not skimmed or partially consulted

statement: If an owning repository has no td database, it is initialized with `td init --work-dir` only after confirming it is a real project repository.

source.quote:
If an owning repository has no td database, initialize it only after confirming it
is a real project repository:

```bash
td init --work-dir /absolute/repo/path
```

scope: an owning repository lacks a td database
trigger: ticket work targets a repository with no td database
outcome: td init runs only after the repository's legitimacy is confirmed, not automatically
notes: Consequence-class sweep: safety — a confirm-before-init gate on a repository-mutating action.

statement: Do not automatically add td instructions to repository guidance files.

source.quote: Do not automatically add td instructions to repository guidance files.

trigger: td is being set up for a repository
outcome: the repository's own guidance files (e.g. AGENTS.md) are left unmodified by this skill
notes: Consequence-class sweep: safety — a never-rule bounding what td initialization is allowed to touch, paralleling sergeant-setup's own guidance-file boundary.

statement: Decisions already approved are not reopened as questions when extracting decisions and unknowns.

source.quote: - Decisions already approved. Do not reopen them as questions.

scope: extracting decisions and unknowns before drafting tickets
trigger: a decision has already been approved
outcome: the approved decision is treated as settled, not re-litigated in the ticket breakdown

statement: A short investigation ticket is created only when an unknown cannot be answered from existing evidence, and it must name the decision or artifact it produces.

source.quote:
Create a short investigation ticket only when an unknown cannot be answered from
existing evidence. Investigation tickets must name the decision or artifact they
produce.

trigger: an unknown is found that genuinely blocks implementation
outcome: an investigation ticket is created only as a last resort, and only with a named deliverable

statement: A ticket's `Blocked by` field lists only tickets that truly prevent starting or merging this work.

source.quote: - **Blocked by**: only tickets that truly prevent starting or merging this work.

trigger: a ticket's `Blocked by` field is being populated
outcome: only genuine blockers are listed, not incidental or convenient orderings
notes: Consequence-class sweep: recovery/delivery — accurate blocking edges are what makes the later frontier computation (L180) trustworthy.

statement: A ticket's `Preserved state` field records the branch, commit, PR, or worktree needed to resume the work.

source.quote: - **Preserved state**: branch, commit, PR, or worktree needed to resume work.

trigger: in-progress or paused work exists that a ticket should let someone resume
outcome: the exact preserved state needed to pick the work back up is recorded on the ticket
notes: Consequence-class sweep: recovery — a durable pointer to resumable state recorded at ticket-definition time.

statement: Vertical slice rules require including every necessary layer for one behavior and forbid creating separate horizontal tickets (e.g. "write backend", "write frontend", "add tests") for that one behavior; a completed ticket must be demoable, testable, or operationally verifiable alone.

source.quote:
- Include every necessary layer for one behavior: storage, API, UI/CLI, tests,
  deployment, and docs only where that slice requires them.
- Do not create separate "write backend", "write frontend", and "add tests"
  horizontal tickets for one behavior.
- A completed ticket must be demoable, testable, or operationally verifiable alone.

trigger: a behavior spans multiple layers (storage, API, UI/CLI, tests)
outcome: one ticket covers the full vertical slice rather than being split by layer, and is independently verifiable when done

statement: Prefactoring is put first only when it materially reduces risk for the slices that follow it.

source.quote: - Put prefactoring first only when it materially reduces risk for following slices.

trigger: a prefactoring step is being considered ahead of feature slices
outcome: prefactoring is ordered first only when it has a real, material risk-reduction justification

statement: Wide refactors follow expand (add the new form beside the old), migrate (move callers in bounded, green batches), then contract (remove the old form after every migration ticket completes).

source.quote:
1. **Expand**: add the new form beside the old.
2. **Migrate**: move callers in bounded, green batches.
3. **Contract**: remove the old form after every migration ticket completes.

scope: a wide mechanical refactor is being broken into tickets
trigger: expand-migrate-contract is the chosen strategy
outcome: the refactor proceeds through three ordered phases rather than one unsafe simultaneous change

statement: Migrate tickets are declared blocked by expand, and the contract ticket is declared blocked by every migration ticket.

source.quote:
Declare all migrate tickets blocked by expand, and contract blocked by every
migration ticket.

scope: wiring dependencies for an expand-migrate-contract breakdown
trigger: expand-migrate-contract tickets are being created
outcome: the dependency graph enforces the phase ordering: migration cannot start before expand, contraction cannot start before every migration completes
notes: Consequence-class sweep: safety — the dependency wiring is what actually prevents contract (a destructive removal of the old form) from running before every caller has migrated.

statement: Unless the user explicitly said to create or publish tickets immediately, the proposed breakdown is presented first, before publishing.

source.quote:
Unless the user explicitly said to create or publish tickets immediately, present
the proposed breakdown first. For every ticket show:

scope: a ticket breakdown has been drafted
trigger: publication has not been explicitly requested immediately
outcome: the user reviews the breakdown before any ticket is actually published
notes: Consequence-class sweep: human-decision — a default review gate before an otherwise-irreversible batch of ticket creation, with a named explicit-instruction override.

statement: When confirming the breakdown, the skill asks only whether granularity, ownership, and blocking edges are correct, and does not ask the user to reconfirm decisions already made.

source.quote:
Ask only whether granularity, ownership, and blocking edges are correct. Do not ask
the user to reconfirm decisions already made.

scope: presenting a ticket breakdown for confirmation
trigger: the breakdown is shown to the user for review
outcome: the confirmation question is scoped narrowly and does not re-litigate settled decisions

statement: Local epics are created first via `td create`, so that child tickets can reference real epic IDs.

source.quote: Create local epics first so child tickets can reference real IDs:

trigger: tickets and their parent epics are being published
outcome: epics exist with real IDs before any child ticket that references them is created

statement: Tickets are created in dependency order, blockers first.

source.quote: Create tickets in dependency order, blockers first:

trigger: multiple interdependent tickets are being created
outcome: a blocking ticket exists in td before any ticket that depends on it is created

statement: For an existing task, the skill updates it rather than creating a duplicate.

source.quote: For an existing task, update rather than duplicate it:

scope: publishing to td when a matching task already exists
trigger: a task matching the new ticket already exists in td
outcome: the existing task is updated in place instead of a second, duplicate task being created
notes: Consequence-class sweep: delivery — the publish-time enforcement of the never-duplicate rule (L23), acting on the dedup check performed earlier (L34).

statement: `sgt-td-create` is used when one approved logical outcome needs matching task records in several registered repositories, with repository-specific details then added via `td log`.

source.quote:
Use `sgt-td-create` when one approved logical outcome needs matching task records in
several registered repositories. Then add repository-specific details with `td log`.

scope: one logical outcome spans several registered repositories
trigger: cross-repository task records are needed for one outcome
outcome: matching records are created together via sgt-td-create, then differentiated per repo with td log

statement: Because td dependencies are repository-local, cross-repository blockers are represented by recording the counterpart repo and td ID in both descriptions or logs and stating the exact merge order, never by inventing a native dependency edge td cannot enforce across databases.

source.quote:
td dependencies are repository-local. For cross-repository blockers:

- Record the counterpart repo and td ID in both descriptions or logs.
- State the exact merge order.
- Do not invent a native dependency edge that td cannot enforce across databases.

scope: a ticket has a blocker in a different repository
trigger: a cross-repository dependency exists
outcome: the dependency is recorded as cross-referenced text and merge order, not as a fabricated native td dependency edge
notes: Consequence-class sweep: safety — an explicit prohibition on fabricating a dependency mechanism the tool cannot actually enforce.

statement: Newly published tasks are not marked `in_progress` by this skill; they remain `open` until dispatch or a worker starts them.

source.quote:
Do not mark tasks `in_progress`; dispatch or a worker does that. New published tasks
remain `open` until work begins.

scope: publishing a new task to td
trigger: a task is being published
outcome: the task's status stays `open`; only dispatch or a worker transitions it to `in_progress`
notes: Consequence-class sweep: identity — the authority to transition a task's state is reserved to dispatch/worker, not the publishing skill itself.

statement: After publishing, the skill confirms no circular or cross-repo pseudo-dependencies exist in the ticket graph.

source.quote: 5. Confirm no circular or cross-repo pseudo-dependencies exist.

trigger: publication has completed
outcome: the dependency graph is checked to be free of cycles and fabricated cross-repo edges before being considered valid
notes: Consequence-class sweep: safety — an integrity check specifically catching a broken graph (cycles, or the fabricated-edge failure mode named at L153) after tickets already exist.

statement: Stale duplicate tickets are closed only with an explicit superseding task, via `td close <duplicate-id> --admin "Superseded by <canonical-id>"`.

source.quote:
7. Close stale duplicates only with an explicit superseding task:

```bash
td close <duplicate-id> --admin "Superseded by <canonical-id>"

scope: a stale duplicate ticket is found during graph validation
trigger: a duplicate is identified after publishing
outcome: the duplicate is closed with an explicit pointer to the ticket that supersedes it, never closed bare

statement: The dispatch frontier reported after publishing consists of the tickets that have no unfinished blockers.

source.quote:
- Ticket IDs grouped by priority and dependency wave.
- The **frontier**: tickets with no unfinished blockers.

trigger: publishing has completed and the frontier is being computed
outcome: only tickets with no remaining blockers are reported as immediately dispatchable

statement: Recommended concurrency defaults to one worker per owning repository, unless the project explicitly supports more.

source.quote:
- Recommended concurrency: one worker per owning repository unless the project
  explicitly supports more.

trigger: the frontier is being reported with a concurrency recommendation
outcome: concurrency stays at one worker per repository unless the project has explicitly opted into more

statement: Dispatch does not happen unless the user asked to begin implementation.

source.quote: Do not dispatch unless the user asked to begin implementation.

scope: after tickets are published and a frontier is reported
trigger: implementation has not been explicitly requested
outcome: no dispatch command is actually run; only the frontier and dispatch commands are reported
notes: Consequence-class sweep: human-decision — publishing tickets and starting implementation are kept as two separately-authorized actions.

statement: A ticket must not include a brittle implementation file list unless a preserved prototype requires it.

source.quote: - [ ] No brittle implementation file list unless a preserved prototype requires it.

scope: reviewing a ticket against the quality checklist before publishing
trigger: a ticket is being checked for readiness
outcome: file lists are excluded from tickets by default, included only when a preserved prototype specifically requires one
